summary: Defines a collection of common data types and groupings in the YANG modeling language, meant to be imported by other modules that model traffic engineering configuration and state.

plainLanguage.summary: A box of shared building blocks that many network configuration descriptions can reuse instead of each making their own.

questions: what are common yang types for traffic engineering
where are te yang groupings defined
what yang modules does rfc 8776 define
subtitle: Two YANG modules of shared building blocks that other traffic engineering models import instead of redefining.

tldr.problem: Many YANG models for traffic engineering (TE) features need the same basic types, such as bandwidth, labels, metrics, administrative groups and path flags. Defining them separately in each model would be repetitive and inconsistent.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two YANG modules, ietf-te-types for generic TE types and groupings and ietf-te-packet-types for packet-specific ones. Other modules import them.
tldr.outcome: Models outside this document can reuse one agreed set of TE types. Technology-specific types for other technologies are outside its scope.

today: RFC 8776 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2020, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Common TE Types
sections.content:
YANG (RFC 6020, RFC 7950) is a data modeling language for configuration data, state data, remote procedure calls and notifications used by management protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241). It has a small set of built-in types and lets authors derive new ones from them.

This RFC introduces a collection of common types and groupings derived from the built-in types. They are meant to be the common pieces for modeling Traffic Engineering (TE) features in models defined outside this document, so it contains no complete device or service model of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every builder inventing their own bricks, everyone gets the same set of bricks to build with.

sections.title: Two Modules and Their Prefixes
sections.content:
The RFC defines two modules. ietf-te-types holds generic TE types that are independent of any specific technology or control-plane instance. ietf-te-packet-types holds the types specific to packet technology. Types for other technologies are out of scope.

Names in the document use the standard prefix of the module they come from, such as yang, inet, rt-types, te-types and te-packet-types. The first three come from RFC 6991 and RFC 8294, which the generic module imports.

Each item is a typedef (a derived type), a grouping (a reusable set of nodes) or an identity (a base that other modules extend). Most of the work is gathering definitions from earlier TE specifications, and the text points at the RFC each came from.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one box of general bricks and one box of special bricks for packet networks. Each brick has a short name tag.

sections.title: The Generic TE Types Module
sections.content:
The ietf-te-types module (revision 2020-06-10) covers several families of definitions.

  • Groupings such as te-bandwidth and te-label, built so each technology can augment them. For unspecified technologies bandwidth is a string and the label is rt-types:generalized-label. Others cover performance metrics and their throttle thresholds, and explicit route hops.
  • Identifiers such as te-global-id, te-node-id (four octets in dotted-quad notation), te-topology-id and te-tp-id, used to name operators, nodes, topologies and link termination points.
  • Link and path attributes such as admin-groups, srlg (a 32-bit number for a Shared Risk Link Group), te-metric, te-link-access-type and te-path-disjointness.
  • Enumerations for loose or strict hops, forward or reverse label direction, and recovery status.
  • Base identities that other modules extend, for path flags, link protection, restoration schemes, association types, objective functions, tunnel types, LSP encodings, switching capabilities and path metric types.

The string form of te-bandwidth is a comma-separated list of numbers. For packet switching it follows the bandwidth-ieee-float32 type from RFC 8294, in bytes per second. For optical networks the same string can carry lists such as ODU counts or frequency slot and width pairs.

The Differentiated Services class type te-ds-class is a number in the range 0..7. The generic administrative group is a hex string of length 1..11.
sections.plainLanguage: The big box has labels for things like how much room a road has, which roads must be avoided together, and what kind of trip is being made.

sections.title: The Packet TE Types Module
sections.content:
The ietf-te-packet-types module imports ietf-te-types and adds definitions that matter for packet networks, mainly around Diffserv-aware TE from RFC 4124.

  • te-class-type: the Diffserv-TE Class-Type, a set of traffic trunks crossing a link that is governed by one set of bandwidth constraints.
  • bc-type: a Diffserv-TE bandwidth constraint, a number in the range 0..7.
  • bc-model-type: a base identity for the supported bandwidth constraints models.
  • backup-protection-type: a base identity for the protection a backup or bypass tunnel can provide.
  • te-bandwidth-requested-type: an enumeration saying whether bandwidth is specified explicitly or auto computed.
  • performance-metrics-attributes-packet: the generic performance metrics plus packet-specific metrics.

The module also defines bandwidth value types with fixed units, such as bandwidth-kbps, bandwidth-mbps and bandwidth-gbps, each an unsigned 64-bit number.
sections.plainLanguage: The second box has bricks made just for roads that carry packets, like labels for how much each kind of traffic may use.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA is asked to register the XML namespaces urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-te-types and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-te-packet-types in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant. It also registers both modules in the YANG Module Names registry, with prefixes te-types and te-packet-types, and RFC 8776 as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The two boxes get official names in a public list so nobody else uses the same names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules define a schema for data accessed over protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH for NETCONF and TLS over HTTPS for RESTCONF. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can limit which users reach which operations and content.

The modules only define types, identities and groupings. Once imported, the resulting schema will have writable or readable data nodes whose access may be sensitive. Unprotected write operations such as edit-config can harm network operations. The security considerations of YANG 1.1 (RFC 7950) also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The bricks are harmless, but anything built with them needs a lock on the door, because changing settings can break the network.
